title: 08 - Political Ideologies

content.text: Syllabus — Political Ideologies: Liberalism, Socialism, Marxism, Fascism, Gandhism, Feminism. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 8) [Gandhism is treated fully in Unit 9.]

the major political ideologies — Liberalism (classical, modern, neo-liberal), Socialism (utopian, revolutionary, evolutionary), Marxism (classical and neo-Marxism), Feminism (its waves and strands) and Fascism — together with Postmodernism and the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ debates. Gandhism is covered in Unit 9.

Locke, Adam Smith, T.H. Green, Hayek, Nozick, Friedman, Rawls, Sen, Lyotard, Foucault, Robert Owen, Bernstein, G.B. Shaw (Fabians), Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao, Gramsci, Marcuse, Althusser, Wollstonecraft, Beauvoir, Betty Friedan, Kate Millett, Mussolini, Hitler, Gentile.

liberalism as a revolutionary idea (2020), end of history (2017), pre-Marxist socialism (2015) & socialism as anti-capitalism (2014), relevance of Marxism (2019), liberal vs radical feminism (2012/2019) & eco-feminism (2017), fascist anti-rationalism, postmodernism (2017).
Q — Trace the evolution of liberalism from classical to modern to neo-liberalism. Was liberalism a revolutionary idea, and is neo-liberalism the ideology of globalization? (UPSC 2020)
Three tasks — define liberalism, prove it was revolutionary, then trace classical → modern → neo-liberal and test the globalization claim.
built on the individual; its five core values are:
— the individual, not the caste, class or community, is the basic unit of politics.
— the supreme value, limited only by the equal freedom of every other individual.
— debate and argument, not tradition or revelation, settle public questions.
— equal moral worth, formal equality before the law and equality of opportunity.
the state may not tell a citizen which god to worship or whom to marry.
destroyed feudal privilege and the divine right of kings.
(Earlier birth fixed your station; liberalism made contract and merit fix it.)
(Like a night guard at a factory gate — he stops theft and violence but never enters the workshop; freedom = nobody interfering.)
: the state ‘hinders the hindrances’ to self-development.
(A starving, illiterate labourer is legally free but unable — hence free schooling and mid-day meals; freedom = ability, not merely absence of restraint.)
(India’s 1991 LPG reforms — licence-raj dismantled, tariffs cut, PSUs disinvested — on the Washington Consensus/WTO 1995 template.)
) revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess.
Liberalism is best understood as a
— a broad ground on which rival doctrines contend — resting on a commitment to the individual.
is acknowledged as its founding father, and the doctrine is built upon five core values:
— the individual, not the caste, class or community, is the basic unit of politics.
— the supreme value of the creed, limited only by the equal freedom of every other individual.
— the conviction that debate and argument, not tradition or revelation, settle public questions.
— the equal moral worth of persons, formal equality before the law and equality of opportunity.
— the state may not prescribe a citizen’s faith or spouse.
In its own age liberalism was genuinely
. By grounding legitimate rule in the

rather than in birth or divinity, it overthrew feudal privilege and the divine right of kings, replacing a hierarchy of status with one of contract and merit. Constitutionalism, natural rights and limited government were the instruments with which it dismantled absolutism — which is why it began life as a doctrine of protest, not of order.
, that is freedom as the absence of interference: like a night guard at a factory gate, the state may prevent theft and violence but never enter the workshop.
: ‘that government is best which governs least’;
recast the state as a ‘source of virtue’ enabling

— the actual capacity for self-development. Green held that ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’ and that it must ‘hinder the hindrances’ to self-realisation: a starving, illiterate labourer is legally free yet unable, so free schooling, mid-day meals and health care become conditions of freedom. This is the philosophical charter of the welfare state.
reverse the movement — ‘rolling back the state’ and ‘market fundamentalism’.
: ‘planning is the road to serfdom’ and ‘social justice is a mirage’;
: freedom is possible only through the market. It duly became globalization’s ideology — Thatcherism and Reaganism, shock therapy, the
and the WTO (1995) — and India’s 1991 liberalisation followed the same template.
Liberalism was a genuinely revolutionary force against absolutism, and it renews itself:

) revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess by insisting that markets be judged by what they do to the worst-off. Its survival lies precisely in this capacity to travel from market-freedom to ‘humane governance’.
Q — Critically examine postmodernism’s ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’ alongside the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ theses. (UPSC 2017)
Explain Lyotard’s attack on grand theories, then test the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ claims against what actually happened.
— a revolt against Modernism, ‘emphasising the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’;
is its father (‘God is dead’, ‘will to power’).
: disbelief in any grand universal theory, for ‘there is not one but many truths’.
(Marxism insists all history must end in communism, liberalism that every society must become a market democracy — one story told for everybody.)
— power/knowledge: ‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’.
— deconstruction: no text has a final meaning.
(The televised event, endlessly replayed, becomes more real to the viewer than the event itself.)
: the post-war welfare-capitalist consensus exhausted the great isms.
(Left and right stopped quarrelling over who owns the factories and quarrelled only over tax rates.)
: the worldwide triumph of liberal democracy after 1991;
— every ‘end’ was premature; and postmodern relativism leaves no ground on which to condemn injustice.

Postmodernism is a rejection of Modernism that ‘emphasises the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’: reason, progress and objective truth — the Enlightenment’s promises — are treated as claims rather than facts.
is regarded as its father, his ‘God is dead’ and ‘will to power’ announcing a world without guaranteed foundations, in which knowledge is always somebody’s knowledge.
gave postmodernism its defining formula: it is

— disbelief in any grand, universal theory that explains everything, ‘for there is not one but many truths’. Marxism holds that all history must culminate in communism and liberalism that every society must end as a market democracy; postmodernism refuses both as single stories imposed on plural human experience.
Three moves give postmodernism its method:
: ‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’, for what counts as knowledge is set by power.
, which dismantles the ‘metaphysics of presence’, denying any final meaning to a text.
, a media world where the image outgrows the thing: the endlessly replayed broadcast becomes more real than the event.

) argued that after the Second World War the great ideological conflicts had exhausted themselves — ‘economics triumphed over politics’ in a welfare-capitalist consensus, and parties argued over tax rates rather than over ownership of the means of production. Critics such as
replied that ‘the end of ideology is itself an ideology’ — a defence of the status quo in neutral dress.
extended the thesis after the Cold War: the ‘worldwide triumph of liberal democracy’ over all rivals marked the end-point of mankind’s ideological evolution — a Hegelian idea.
countered with the ‘clash of civilizations’: future conflict would be driven by ethnic, religious and civilisational identity, not by ideology.

All three theses proclaim an ‘end’ — of universal truth, of ideology, of history — yet the resurgence of nationalism, religious politics and gross inequality refutes them. Postmodernism usefully warns against dogmatic metanarratives and recovers marginalised voices, but its own relativism risks leaving no firm ground from which injustice can be criticised at all.
Q — Distinguish revolutionary from evolutionary socialism; assess pre-Marxist (utopian) socialism and whether socialism may be reborn as anti-capitalism. (UPSC 2015/2014)
Three demands — separate utopian from scientific socialism, contrast the revolutionary and evolutionary roads, then ask what survives today.
— opposition to capitalism; its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and cooperation over competition.
: ‘a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’.
(the utopians painted the destination — a model village — but drew no road to it; Marx claimed to supply the laws of capitalism’s collapse, hence ‘scientific’)
— the Marxist road: abolish capitalism ‘in a single stroke’, since the state is a class instrument that cannot be borrowed by the workers.
— the gradual, parliamentary road, in four variants:
: workers armed with the vote need no revolution.
(It reached India as Nehruvian socialism — a mixed economy built by Parliament and the Five-Year Plans, not by barricades.)
— workers’ control through militant trade unions and the general strike.
: industry run by self-governing guilds rather than by the state.
, Occupy Wall Street, the Yellow Vests,
— charged with being capitalism’s ‘safety valve’, socialism now survives less as a programme of power than as the moral vocabulary of the fight against inequality.

Socialism is defined by its opposition to capitalism: its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and it prefers cooperation to competition, holding human beings to be social creatures shaped by their conditions rather than self-seeking atoms. Because it has been claimed by so many,
quipped that ‘socialism is like a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’.
because they painted an ideal destination without analysing capitalism or charting the road to it, appealing merely to the goodwill of the rich; his own socialism claimed to be
, deriving socialism from the laws of capitalist development itself. The three great pre-Marxist socialists were:
— who first used the word ‘socialist’ and proposed ‘villages of cooperation’.
— who would reorganise labour so as to make work pleasant.

The Marxist tradition holds that capitalism must be overthrown ‘in a single stroke’ and replaced by a classless society, since the existing state is an instrument of the propertied class and cannot simply be captured and used by the workers. Reform, on this view, only repairs the machine of exploitation; hence the dictatorship of the proletariat as a transitional necessity.
The democratic-socialist tradition proceeds gradually and parliamentarily, and took four principal forms:
argued that workers armed with the vote need no revolution, capitalism having failed to polarise society as Marx foretold.
preached the ‘inevitability of gradualness’ and inspired Nehruvian socialism, a mixed economy built through Parliament and the Five-Year Plans.
— sought workers’ control through militant trade unions and the general strike rather than through the state.
would vest industry in self-governing guilds of producers, avoiding both the market and the bureaucratic state.
With inequality rising, socialism revives less as a state project than as an anti-capitalist critique:
, movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, and
stark alternative, ‘socialism or barbarism’, all attack concentrated wealth without promising a seizure of power.

Evolutionary socialism made socialism democratically respectable but stands charged with legitimising the bourgeois state — a ‘safety valve’ that releases pressure without changing ownership. Its twenty-first-century relevance therefore lies not in capturing power but in supplying the moral vocabulary of the struggle against inequality: socialism reborn as anti-capitalism.
Q — Explain the main tenets of Marxism (dialectical and historical materialism, class conflict, surplus value) and evaluate its contemporary relevance. (UPSC 2019)
Set out Marxism’s philosophical core — materialism, class conflict, exploitation — and then judge honestly what survives of it.
gave socialism a ‘scientific’ basis: history is the conflict of antagonistic classes over who owns production.
thesis–antithesis–synthesis, but matter not idea is the essence of reality.
(Hegel stood on his head: not ideas but the loom, the mill and the mine make history move.)
; stages run slave → feudal → capitalist → socialist → communist.
(Who owns the land and the factory decides whose law, morality and religion prevail.)
— ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’; the proletariat is ‘the only really revolutionary class’.
a worker paid Rs 300 a day may add Rs 900 of value to the cloth: the unpaid Rs 600 is surplus value.
owning neither the product nor the pace of his work, he is alienated from his own labour.
— predictions failed and regimes collapsed, yet 2008,
— discredited as a blueprint for revolution, indispensable as a

, claims to place socialism on a ‘scientific’ footing by deriving it from the laws of social development rather than from moral aspiration. Its organising insight is that every society is divided by the ownership of the means of production into antagonistic classes, and that this conflict, not the deeds of great men, is the motor of history.

dialectic — thesis, antithesis, synthesis — with materialism: matter, not idea, is the essence of reality, so Hegel is famously stood on his head. Not philosophy but the loom, the mill and the mine make history move, and each social order generates within itself the contradiction that destroys it.
formalised its three laws, including the transformation of quantity into quality.
Applied to society, this yields the
(forces plus relations of production) determines the

of law, politics, religion and ideas — who owns the land and the factory decides whose law and whose morality prevail. History therefore advances through stages: primitive communism, slave, feudal, capitalist, socialist and finally communist society, each transition driven by a clash between new productive forces and old relations.
4. Class struggle, surplus value and alienation.
Three linked tenets carry the analysis of capitalism:

— ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’, and the proletariat is ‘the only really revolutionary class’; when the ‘class in itself’ becomes a ‘class for itself’, revolution follows.
— the measure of exploitation: labour alone creates value, so a worker paid Rs 300 a day who adds Rs 900 of value to the cloth surrenders Rs 600 unpaid to the capitalist.
— its human cost: owning neither the product nor the pace of his work, the worker is estranged from his labour, his fellows and himself.
Marxism’s specific predictions — imminent revolution in the advanced West, the progressive immiseration of the workers — largely failed, and the state-socialist regimes collapsed after 1989. Yet its
) defends its core, and the crash of 2008 and Occupy Wall Street echoed its concerns.
As a blueprint for revolution Marxism stands largely discredited; as a

for exploitation, alienation and structural inequality it remains strikingly relevant. That is why every crisis of capitalism sends readers back to Marx, even where nobody expects the proletarian revolution he foretold.
Q — How did neo-Marxism (Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Althusser) reformulate the base–superstructure relationship?
Explain why revolution never came in the West — and how Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and Althusser rebuilt Marxism around culture.
— classical Marxism made the superstructure a mere reflection of the economic base, yet the advanced West did not revolt; neo-Marxism rescues Marxism from this ‘crude economic determinism’.
: the ruling class rules by consent manufactured in
(School, temple, cinema and newspaper teach the poor that the existing order is natural ‘common sense’ — consent, not the police, keeps it standing.)
— the exploited think in their masters’ categories, so
must first win the battle of ideas.
(The worker who votes for his employer’s party has borrowed his employer’s worldview.)
— Marxism recast as a critique of culture and domination rather than of economics.
— art and leisure turned into standardised commodities that pacify.
: capitalism manufactures ‘false needs’ and absorbs dissent.
(It sells the discontented a new phone instead of a new society.)
— the base determines only ‘in the last instance’; two devices do the work:
— family, school, religion and media reproduce the relations of production.
— the battleground shifts from the economy to culture and consciousness, explaining capitalism’s durability.
— ideas, law, culture, the state — as a mere reflection of the economic
, and expected revolution first in the most advanced capitalist societies. When it arrived instead in agrarian Russia and China while the Western worker grew reformist,
rescued Marxism from this ‘crude economic determinism’ by granting the superstructure a life and a power of its own.
, the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, argued that the ruling class rules not by coercion alone but by
— intellectual and moral leadership manufactured through

: school, church, press and popular culture. Through them the existing distribution of property comes to look like natural ‘common sense’, so that consent rather than the policeman keeps the order standing.
3. False consciousness and the war of position.

: the exploited understand their own condition in categories supplied by their exploiters — the worker who votes for his employer’s party has borrowed his employer’s worldview. Revolution therefore requires first a
, a long ideological struggle in which
thrown up by the working class build a counter-hegemony, before any frontal ‘war of manoeuvre’ can succeed.
— Marxism recast as a critique of culture, reason and domination rather than of economics alone.
— art and leisure are turned into standardised commodities that pacify rather than provoke.
shows how advanced capitalism manufactures ‘false needs’ and absorbs dissent — selling the discontented a new phone instead of a new society — so that opposition itself becomes a commodity.

, of the structuralist school, allowed each level relative autonomy in a ‘multi-sectoral’ analysis, the economy being determinant only ‘in the last instance’. Two devices carry his account of ideology:
— family, school, religion and media, which reproduce the relations of production far more quietly than the repressive apparatus of army and police.
— the process by which ideology ‘hails’ individuals and constitutes them as obedient subjects.
Neo-Marxism shifted the decisive battleground from the

. In doing so it explained capitalism’s remarkable durability and reshaped Marxism into a theory of ideology and hegemony rather than of inevitable economic collapse — the form in which Marxism still influences media studies, education and cultural politics today.
Q — Why is the sex/gender distinction central to feminist analysis? Distinguish liberal, socialist and radical feminism and the waves of feminism. (UPSC 2012/2019)
Two halves — why sex/gender is the foundation of feminist argument, and how the strands and the three waves differ.
— feminism rests on two beliefs: ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’.
: ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’.
(Sex is who bears the child; gender is the rule that the daughter cooks while the son studies.)
: equal legal and political rights within the system, since gender is ‘irrelevant to public life’.
(Equal education, the vote, equal pay for equal work.)
(The unpaid cooking and care that sends the wage-earner back to work each morning costs capital nothing.)
— women’s liberation and the private sphere.
— the distinction converts subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice; the strands differ only on the cure.

Feminist ideology rests on two beliefs — ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’. The first is descriptive and the second normative, which is why feminism is simultaneously a theory of society and a movement for its transformation, cutting across liberal, socialist and radical traditions rather than belonging to any one of them.
is a cultural construct of masculine and feminine roles that society imposes and can therefore unmake. As

put it, ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’: sex is who bears the child, gender is the household rule that the daughter cooks while the son studies. This shatters the claim that ‘biology is destiny’ and converts subordination into a social wrong.
A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

are reformist: gender is ‘irrelevant to public life’, so women need equal education, the vote, equal legal personality and equal pay within the existing order. Critics answer that formal equality leaves the unequal burdens of the home untouched, and that it speaks chiefly for educated middle-class women.
Both go beyond legal equality to a structural explanation of women’s subordination, but locate its root differently:
: women form a ‘reserve army of labour’ and their unpaid domestic work reproduces labour power free of cost to capital.
is itself the root, prior to class — ‘the personal is political’ — so family, marriage and sexuality must be transformed, not merely property.
The movement is conventionally divided into three phases:
— the suffrage movement, winning legal personality and the vote.
— ‘women’s liberation’, which carried the struggle into the private sphere:
‘problem with no name’ named the discontent of the suburban housewife.
— the politics of difference, expressed through black, postcolonial and eco-feminism.

The sex/gender distinction is the theoretical foundation of every feminist strand because it turns women’s subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice. What divides feminists is only the cure — equal rights, the end of capitalism, or the overthrow of patriarchy — not the diagnosis that gender is made, and therefore can be unmade.
Q — “One is not born, but becomes, a woman.” Examine radical feminism and patriarchy, and evaluate eco-feminism and the newer strands (black, postcolonial). (UPSC 2017)
Unpack Beauvoir’s line through radical feminism’s theory of patriarchy, then weigh the eco-, black and postcolonial challenges to it.
: a system in which ‘male shall dominate female, elder male shall dominate younger’, prior to class or race.
(Its unit is the family: property, surname and authority descend from father to son.)
— the private sphere is itself a structure of power.
(Who eats last, who does the unpaid housework, who decides a pregnancy — all are questions of politics, not of affection.)
: woman is defined only against man, so she is made, not born;
: woman and nature are both treated as passive resources.
(The Indian village woman who fetches the water and gathers the fuel is the first to suffer when the forest and the stream are destroyed.)
— mainstream feminism universalised the white middle-class woman and ignored race and class; two challengers:
: race and class cut across any common sisterhood.
: the ‘third-world woman’ cannot be spoken for by Western feminists.
— feminism moves from sisterhood-as-sameness to a
Radical feminism, the defining strand of the
— literally ‘rule by the father’ — is the most fundamental and universal form of oppression, older and deeper than class or race.

defines it as a system in which ‘male shall dominate female, elder male shall dominate younger’; its basic unit is the family, through which property, surname and authority descend from father to son.

, denies the liberal separation of public and private: the family, marriage, housework and sexuality are themselves structures of power. Who eats last, who performs the unpaid domestic labour and who decides a pregnancy are political questions, not matters of private affection — which is why domestic violence and marital rape became feminist causes rather than family secrets.
) argues that man is posited as the norm and woman defined only in relation to him — the
— so that ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’: femininity is manufactured by upbringing, not given by nature.
pressed the argument further, calling rape ‘an institution of patriarchy’, and some radicals advocate androgyny as the escape.

: a masculinist, exploitative order treats both as passive resources to be used up. For Shiva the Indian village woman who fetches the water and gathers the fuel is the first casualty when forest and stream are destroyed, which makes women the natural allies of ecology.
Both charge that mainstream white, middle-class feminism universalised one experience and ignored
argues that the woman who must also fight poverty, caste and racism does not share the suburban housewife’s agenda.
holds that the ‘third-world woman’, burdened by a colonial legacy, cannot be spoken for by Western feminists.

Radical feminism transformed the discipline by politicising the private sphere, but its assumption of a single ‘women’s experience’ — an ‘essential’ femininity — is exactly what eco-, black and postcolonial feminists contest. Feminism has accordingly moved from sisterhood-as-sameness to a
Q — Is fascism a coherent ideology? Discuss its anti-rationalism and core tenets, its conception of the state, and whether it was merely an inter-war phenomenon.
Test whether fascism is an ideology at all — its anti-rational core, its state, and whether it died in 1945.
, ‘strength through unity’: ‘the individual, in a literal sense, is nothing’; a ‘hodge-podge of ideologies’ rather than a system.
(No founding text answers to Marx’s Capital or Locke’s Treatises.)
— a counter-Enlightenment cult of will, instinct and myth over reason:
(Torchlit parades, uniforms and the myth of national rebirth move the crowd where argument cannot.)
— social Darwinism: ‘war is to men what maternity is to women’.
— chauvinistic, ranking nations as organic and unequal wholes.
: ‘nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it’.
(State-licensed bodies of employers and workers replace free trade unions — class conflict abolished by decree.)
— ties it to defeat, depression and fear of communism, so it died with its epoch.
— to the ‘fear of freedom’ in human nature, which implies recurrence.
— not a coherent ideology but a reactive movement; its impulses recur wherever crisis breeds authoritarian nationalism.
Fascism takes its name from the

, the bundle of rods symbolising ‘strength through unity’, and subordinates the individual utterly to nation and state — ‘the individual, in a literal sense, is nothing’ — aiming to forge a ‘new man’ of duty and sacrifice. Having no founding text comparable to
, it is commonly dismissed as a ‘
’ or a ‘political religion’ rather than a coherent doctrine.
is its hallmark: a counter-Enlightenment cult of

‘political myths’ supply the model — a belief is judged by its power to mobilise, not by its truth — and Mussolini preferred ‘action, not talk’, declaring that ‘1789 is dead’. Torchlit parades, uniforms and the myth of national rebirth were deliberately chosen to move crowds where argument could not.
Its other tenets follow, among them the pseudo-radical appeal of ‘national socialism’:
— conflict as the law of life, a social Darwinism in which ‘war is to men what maternity is to women’.
— the Führerprinzip, by which the leader embodies the will of the people, drawing on
— a chauvinistic creed that ranks nations as organic and unequal wholes.

there is ‘nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it’, an inheritance from Hegel’s worship of the state. Corporatism means that state-licensed bodies of employers and workers replace free trade unions, so class conflict is abolished by decree rather than resolved. Nazism added
— Aryan supremacy, anti-Semitism and the ‘final solution’.
— treats fascism as the product of specific
— military defeat, the Depression, wounded national pride and fear of communism — so that it died with its epoch.
— locates it instead in human nature, in the ‘fear of freedom’ that tempts the insecure individual to surrender himself to an authority, which implies recurrence.
— offers the Marxist reading: ‘a desperate attempt by capitalism to protect itself’.

Fascism is best seen not as a coherent ideology but as a reactive, anti-rational movement of extreme nationalism and leader-worship, held together by enemies rather than by principles. Fromm’s ‘fear of freedom’ is the warning: it was no mere inter-war accident, and its impulses resurface wherever crisis breeds authoritarian nationalism.
core values: individualism, freedom, reason, justice, toleration.
classical (Locke/Smith, night-watchman) → modern (Green, positive liberty) → neo-liberal (Hayek/Nozick/Friedman).

Joad — ‘a hat that has lost its shape’; core value = social equality.
dialectical + historical materialism; base→superstructure; class struggle; surplus value.

sex (biological) vs gender (social); Beauvoir — ‘one is not born but becomes a woman’.
1st suffrage; 2nd women’s liberation (Friedan’s ‘problem with no name’); 3rd difference (black/postcolonial).
fasces = strength through unity; anti-rationalism; ‘1789 is dead’; totalitarian corporatist state.
revolutionary (vs feudalism); classical→modern→neo-liberal; neo-liberalism = globalization’s ideology; social-liberal revival.
Lyotard ‘incredulity to metanarratives’; Bell (end of ideology), Fukuyama (end of history) vs Huntington.

contentText: Syllabus — Political Ideologies: Liberalism, Socialism, Marxism, Fascism, Gandhism, Feminism. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 8) [Gandhism is treated fully in Unit 9.] Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the major political ideologies — Liberalism (classical, modern, neo-liberal), Socialism (utopian, revolutionary, evolutionary), Marxism (classical and neo-Marxism), Feminism (its waves and strands) and Fascism — together with Postmodernism and the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ debates. Gandhism is covered in Unit 9. Must-know thinkers:  Locke, Adam Smith, T.H. Green, Hayek, Nozick, Friedman, Rawls, Sen, Lyotard, Foucault, Robert Owen, Bernstein, G.B. Shaw (Fabians), Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao, Gramsci, Marcuse, Althusser, Wollstonecraft, Beauvoir, Betty Friedan, Kate Millett, Mussolini, Hitler, Gentile. PYQ trend:  liberalism as a revolutionary idea (2020), end of history (2017), pre-Marxist socialism (2015) & socialism as anti-capitalism (2014), relevance of Marxism (2019), liberal vs radical feminism (2012/2019) & eco-feminism (2017), fascist anti-rationalism, postmodernism (2017). Master Questions Q — Trace the evolution of liberalism from classical to modern to neo-liberalism. Was liberalism a revolutionary idea, and is neo-liberalism the ideology of globalization? (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Three tasks — define liberalism, prove it was revolutionary, then trace classical → modern → neo-liberal and test the globalization claim. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  — a  meta-ideology  built on the individual; its five core values are:    1.1 Individualism  — the individual, not the caste, class or community, is the basic unit of politics.    1.2 Freedom  — the supreme value, limited only by the equal freedom of every other individual.    1.3 Reason  — debate and argument, not tradition or revelation, settle public questions.    1.4 Justice  — equal moral worth, formal equality before the law and equality of opportunity.    1.5 Toleration  —  the state may not tell a citizen which god to worship or whom to marry. 2. Revolutionary  — rule grounded in the  consent of the people  destroyed feudal privilege and the divine right of kings.  (Earlier birth fixed your station; liberalism made contract and merit fix it.) 3. Classical  —  Locke, Smith, Spencer : the  night-watchman state  and  negative liberty .  (Like a night guard at a factory gate — he stops theft and violence but never enters the workshop; freedom = nobody interfering.) 4. Modern / positive  —  Green, Hobhouse, Laski : the state ‘hinders the hindrances’ to self-development.  (A starving, illiterate labourer is legally free but unable — hence free schooling and mid-day meals; freedom = ability, not merely absence of restraint.) 5. Neo-liberalism  —  Hayek, Nozick, Friedman : ‘roll back the state’, market fundamentalism.  (India’s 1991 LPG reforms — licence-raj dismantled, tariffs cut, PSUs disinvested — on the Washington Consensus/WTO 1995 template.) 6. Conclusion  —  social liberalism  ( Rawls, Sen, Stiglitz ) revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess. Model Answer 1. Core.  Liberalism is best understood as a  meta-ideology  — a broad ground on which rival doctrines contend — resting on a commitment to the individual.  Locke  is acknowledged as its founding father, and the doctrine is built upon five core values:    1.1 Individualism  — the individual, not the caste, class or community, is the basic unit of politics.    1.2 Freedom  — the supreme value of the creed, limited only by the equal freedom of every other individual.    1.3 Reason  — the conviction that debate and argument, not tradition or revelation, settle public questions.    1.4 Justice  — the equal moral worth of persons, formal equality before the law and equality of opportunity.    1.5 Toleration  — the state may not prescribe a citizen’s faith or spouse. 2. Revolutionary.  In its own age liberalism was genuinely  revolutionary . By grounding legitimate rule in the  consent of the people  rather than in birth or divinity, it overthrew feudal privilege and the divine right of kings, replacing a hierarchy of status with one of contract and merit. Constitutionalism, natural rights and limited government were the instruments with which it dismantled absolutism — which is why it began life as a doctrine of protest, not of order. 3. Classical liberalism.  Locke  — the ‘father of classical liberalism’ — with  Adam Smith  and  Herbert Spencer  champions the minimal ‘ night-watchman ’ state, laissez-faire, natural rights and  negative liberty , that is freedom as the absence of interference: like a night guard at a factory gate, the state may prevent theft and violence but never enter the workshop.  Jefferson : ‘that government is best which governs least’;  Macpherson  labels its individual ‘possessive’. 4. Modern / positive liberalism.  T.H. Green ,  Hobhouse  and  Laski  recast the state as a ‘source of virtue’ enabling  positive liberty  — the actual capacity for self-development. Green held that ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’ and that it must ‘hinder the hindrances’ to self-realisation: a starving, illiterate labourer is legally free yet unable, so free schooling, mid-day meals and health care become conditions of freedom. This is the philosophical charter of the welfare state. 5. Neo-liberalism.  Hayek ,  Nozick  ( Anarchy, State and Utopia ) and  Friedman  reverse the movement — ‘rolling back the state’ and ‘market fundamentalism’.  Hayek : ‘planning is the road to serfdom’ and ‘social justice is a mirage’;  Friedman : freedom is possible only through the market. It duly became globalization’s ideology — Thatcherism and Reaganism, shock therapy, the  Washington Consensus  and the WTO (1995) — and India’s 1991 liberalisation followed the same template. 6. Conclusion.  Liberalism was a genuinely revolutionary force against absolutism, and it renews itself:  social liberalism  ( Rawls, Sen, Stiglitz ) revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess by insisting that markets be judged by what they do to the worst-off. Its survival lies precisely in this capacity to travel from market-freedom to ‘humane governance’. Q — Critically examine postmodernism’s ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’ alongside the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ theses. (UPSC 2017) What it’s asking:  Explain Lyotard’s attack on grand theories, then test the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ claims against what actually happened. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What it is  — a revolt against Modernism, ‘emphasising the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’;  Nietzsche  is its father (‘God is dead’, ‘will to power’). 2. Incredulity towards metanarratives  —  Lyotard : disbelief in any grand universal theory, for ‘there is not one but many truths’.  (Marxism insists all history must end in communism, liberalism that every society must become a market democracy — one story told for everybody.) 3. Key moves  — three postmodern instruments:    3.1  Foucault  — power/knowledge: ‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’.    3.2  Derrida  — deconstruction: no text has a final meaning.    3.3  Baudrillard  — hyper-reality.  (The televised event, endlessly replayed, becomes more real to the viewer than the event itself.) 4. End of ideology  —  Bell : the post-war welfare-capitalist consensus exhausted the great isms.  (Left and right stopped quarrelling over who owns the factories and quarrelled only over tax rates.) 5. End of history  —  Fukuyama : the worldwide triumph of liberal democracy after 1991;  Huntington  replies with the ‘clash of civilizations’. 6. Conclusion  — every ‘end’ was premature; and postmodern relativism leaves no ground on which to condemn injustice. Model Answer 1. What it is.  Postmodernism is a rejection of Modernism that ‘emphasises the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’: reason, progress and objective truth — the Enlightenment’s promises — are treated as claims rather than facts.  Nietzsche  is regarded as its father, his ‘God is dead’ and ‘will to power’ announcing a world without guaranteed foundations, in which knowledge is always somebody’s knowledge. 2. Incredulity towards metanarratives.  Jean-Francois Lyotard  gave postmodernism its defining formula: it is  ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’  — disbelief in any grand, universal theory that explains everything, ‘for there is not one but many truths’. Marxism holds that all history must culminate in communism and liberalism that every society must end as a market democracy; postmodernism refuses both as single stories imposed on plural human experience. 3. Key moves.  Three moves give postmodernism its method:    3.1  Foucault  —  power/knowledge : ‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’, for what counts as knowledge is set by power.    3.2  Derrida  —  deconstruction , which dismantles the ‘metaphysics of presence’, denying any final meaning to a text.    3.3  Baudrillard  —  hyper-reality , a media world where the image outgrows the thing: the endlessly replayed broadcast becomes more real than the event. 4. End of ideology.  Daniel Bell  (with  Lipset  and  Dahrendorf ) argued that after the Second World War the great ideological conflicts had exhausted themselves — ‘economics triumphed over politics’ in a welfare-capitalist consensus, and parties argued over tax rates rather than over ownership of the means of production. Critics such as  Macpherson  and  MacIntyre  replied that ‘the end of ideology is itself an ideology’ — a defence of the status quo in neutral dress. 5. End of history.  Francis Fukuyama  extended the thesis after the Cold War: the ‘worldwide triumph of liberal democracy’ over all rivals marked the end-point of mankind’s ideological evolution — a Hegelian idea.  Samuel Huntington  countered with the ‘clash of civilizations’: future conflict would be driven by ethnic, religious and civilisational identity, not by ideology. 6. Conclusion.  All three theses proclaim an ‘end’ — of universal truth, of ideology, of history — yet the resurgence of nationalism, religious politics and gross inequality refutes them. Postmodernism usefully warns against dogmatic metanarratives and recovers marginalised voices, but its own relativism risks leaving no firm ground from which injustice can be criticised at all. Q — Distinguish revolutionary from evolutionary socialism; assess pre-Marxist (utopian) socialism and whether socialism may be reborn as anti-capitalism. (UPSC 2015/2014) What it’s asking:  Three demands — separate utopian from scientific socialism, contrast the revolutionary and evolutionary roads, then ask what survives today. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  — opposition to capitalism; its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and cooperation over competition.  Joad : ‘a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’. 2. Utopian vs scientific  —  (the utopians painted the destination — a model village — but drew no road to it; Marx claimed to supply the laws of capitalism’s collapse, hence ‘scientific’) . The three pre-Marxist utopians:    2.1  Owen  — ‘villages of cooperation’.    2.2  Fourier  — work made pleasant.    2.3  Saint-Simon  — rule by scientific ‘luminaries’. 3. Revolutionary socialism  — the Marxist road: abolish capitalism ‘in a single stroke’, since the state is a class instrument that cannot be borrowed by the workers. 4. Evolutionary socialism  — the gradual, parliamentary road, in four variants:    4.1 Revisionism  —  Bernstein : workers armed with the vote need no revolution.    4.2 Fabianism  —  Shaw, the Webbs : the ‘inevitability of gradualness’.  (It reached India as Nehruvian socialism — a mixed economy built by Parliament and the Five-Year Plans, not by barricades.)    4.3 Syndicalism  — workers’ control through militant trade unions and the general strike.    4.4 Guild socialism  —  Cole : industry run by self-governing guilds rather than by the state. 5. Rebirth as anti-capitalism  —  Miliband’s   Socialism for a Sceptical Age , Occupy Wall Street, the Yellow Vests,  Wallerstein’s  ‘socialism or barbarism’. 6. Conclusion  — charged with being capitalism’s ‘safety valve’, socialism now survives less as a programme of power than as the moral vocabulary of the fight against inequality. Model Answer 1. Core.  Socialism is defined by its opposition to capitalism: its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and it prefers cooperation to competition, holding human beings to be social creatures shaped by their conditions rather than self-seeking atoms. Because it has been claimed by so many,  C.E.M. Joad  quipped that ‘socialism is like a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’. 2. Utopian versus scientific.  Marx dismissed his predecessors as  ‘utopian’  because they painted an ideal destination without analysing capitalism or charting the road to it, appealing merely to the goodwill of the rich; his own socialism claimed to be  scientific , deriving socialism from the laws of capitalist development itself. The three great pre-Marxist socialists were:    2.1  Robert Owen  — who first used the word ‘socialist’ and proposed ‘villages of cooperation’.    2.2  Charles Fourier  — who would reorganise labour so as to make work pleasant.    2.3  Saint-Simon  — who favoured rule by scientific ‘luminaries’. 3. Revolutionary socialism.  The Marxist tradition holds that capitalism must be overthrown ‘in a single stroke’ and replaced by a classless society, since the existing state is an instrument of the propertied class and cannot simply be captured and used by the workers. Reform, on this view, only repairs the machine of exploitation; hence the dictatorship of the proletariat as a transitional necessity. 4. Evolutionary socialism.  The democratic-socialist tradition proceeds gradually and parliamentarily, and took four principal forms:    4.1 Revisionism  —  Eduard Bernstein  argued that workers armed with the vote need no revolution, capitalism having failed to polarise society as Marx foretold.    4.2 Fabianism  —  G.B. Shaw  and  the Webbs  preached the ‘inevitability of gradualness’ and inspired Nehruvian socialism, a mixed economy built through Parliament and the Five-Year Plans.    4.3 Syndicalism  — sought workers’ control through militant trade unions and the general strike rather than through the state.    4.4 Guild socialism  —  G.D.H. Cole  would vest industry in self-governing guilds of producers, avoiding both the market and the bureaucratic state. 5. Rebirth as anti-capitalism.  With inequality rising, socialism revives less as a state project than as an anti-capitalist critique:  Ralph Miliband’s   Socialism for a Sceptical Age , movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, and  Wallerstein’s  stark alternative, ‘socialism or barbarism’, all attack concentrated wealth without promising a seizure of power. 6. Conclusion.  Evolutionary socialism made socialism democratically respectable but stands charged with legitimising the bourgeois state — a ‘safety valve’ that releases pressure without changing ownership. Its twenty-first-century relevance therefore lies not in capturing power but in supplying the moral vocabulary of the struggle against inequality: socialism reborn as anti-capitalism. Q — Explain the main tenets of Marxism (dialectical and historical materialism, class conflict, surplus value) and evaluate its contemporary relevance. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Set out Marxism’s philosophical core — materialism, class conflict, exploitation — and then judge honestly what survives of it. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  —  Marx  and  Engels  gave socialism a ‘scientific’ basis: history is the conflict of antagonistic classes over who owns production. 2. Dialectical materialism  —  Hegel’s  thesis–antithesis–synthesis, but matter not idea is the essence of reality.  (Hegel stood on his head: not ideas but the loom, the mill and the mine make history move.) 3. Historical materialism  — the economic  base  determines the  superstructure ; stages run slave → feudal → capitalist → socialist → communist.  (Who owns the land and the factory decides whose law, morality and religion prevail.) 4. Class struggle, surplus value, alienation  — three linked tenets:    4.1 Class struggle  — ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’; the proletariat is ‘the only really revolutionary class’.    4.2 Surplus value  —  a worker paid Rs 300 a day may add Rs 900 of value to the cloth: the unpaid Rs 600 is surplus value.    4.3 Alienation  —  owning neither the product nor the pace of his work, he is alienated from his own labour. 5. Relevance  — predictions failed and regimes collapsed, yet 2008,  Piketty  and  Eagleton  revived the critique of capitalism. 6. Conclusion  — discredited as a blueprint for revolution, indispensable as a  diagnostic tool  for exploitation and inequality. Model Answer 1. Core.  Marxism, founded by  Karl Marx  and  Friedrich Engels , claims to place socialism on a ‘scientific’ footing by deriving it from the laws of social development rather than from moral aspiration. Its organising insight is that every society is divided by the ownership of the means of production into antagonistic classes, and that this conflict, not the deeds of great men, is the motor of history. 2. Dialectical materialism.  Marx fuses  Hegel’s  dialectic — thesis, antithesis, synthesis — with materialism: matter, not idea, is the essence of reality, so Hegel is famously stood on his head. Not philosophy but the loom, the mill and the mine make history move, and each social order generates within itself the contradiction that destroys it.  Engels  formalised its three laws, including the transformation of quantity into quality. 3. Historical materialism.  Applied to society, this yields the  base–superstructure  model: the economic  base  (forces plus relations of production) determines the  superstructure  of law, politics, religion and ideas — who owns the land and the factory decides whose law and whose morality prevail. History therefore advances through stages: primitive communism, slave, feudal, capitalist, socialist and finally communist society, each transition driven by a clash between new productive forces and old relations. 4. Class struggle, surplus value and alienation.  Three linked tenets carry the analysis of capitalism:    4.1 Class struggle  — ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’, and the proletariat is ‘the only really revolutionary class’; when the ‘class in itself’ becomes a ‘class for itself’, revolution follows.    4.2 Surplus value  — the measure of exploitation: labour alone creates value, so a worker paid Rs 300 a day who adds Rs 900 of value to the cloth surrenders Rs 600 unpaid to the capitalist.    4.3 Alienation  — its human cost: owning neither the product nor the pace of his work, the worker is estranged from his labour, his fellows and himself. 5. Contemporary relevance.  Marxism’s specific predictions — imminent revolution in the advanced West, the progressive immiseration of the workers — largely failed, and the state-socialist regimes collapsed after 1989. Yet its  critique of capitalism  endures:  Thomas Piketty  ( Capital in the Twenty-First Century ) documents widening inequality,  Terry Eagleton  ( Why Marx Was Right ) defends its core, and the crash of 2008 and Occupy Wall Street echoed its concerns. 6. Conclusion.  As a blueprint for revolution Marxism stands largely discredited; as a  diagnostic tool  for exploitation, alienation and structural inequality it remains strikingly relevant. That is why every crisis of capitalism sends readers back to Marx, even where nobody expects the proletarian revolution he foretold. Q — How did neo-Marxism (Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Althusser) reformulate the base–superstructure relationship? What it’s asking:  Explain why revolution never came in the West — and how Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and Althusser rebuilt Marxism around culture. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The problem  — classical Marxism made the superstructure a mere reflection of the economic base, yet the advanced West did not revolt; neo-Marxism rescues Marxism from this ‘crude economic determinism’. 2. Hegemony  —  Gramsci : the ruling class rules by consent manufactured in  civil society .  (School, temple, cinema and newspaper teach the poor that the existing order is natural ‘common sense’ — consent, not the police, keeps it standing.) 3. False consciousness & war of position  — the exploited think in their masters’ categories, so  organic intellectuals  must first win the battle of ideas.  (The worker who votes for his employer’s party has borrowed his employer’s worldview.) 4. Frankfurt School  —  Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse ; three contributions:    4.1 Critical theory  — Marxism recast as a critique of culture and domination rather than of economics.    4.2 The ‘culture industry’  — art and leisure turned into standardised commodities that pacify.    4.3 One-dimensional man  —  Marcuse : capitalism manufactures ‘false needs’ and absorbs dissent.  (It sells the discontented a new phone instead of a new society.) 5. Althusser  — the base determines only ‘in the last instance’; two devices do the work:    5.1 Ideological state apparatuses  — family, school, religion and media reproduce the relations of production.    5.2 Interpellation  — ideology ‘hails’ individuals into obedient subjects. 6. Conclusion  — the battleground shifts from the economy to culture and consciousness, explaining capitalism’s durability. Model Answer 1. The problem.  Classical Marxism treated the  superstructure  — ideas, law, culture, the state — as a mere reflection of the economic  base , and expected revolution first in the most advanced capitalist societies. When it arrived instead in agrarian Russia and China while the Western worker grew reformist,  neo-Marxists  rescued Marxism from this ‘crude economic determinism’ by granting the superstructure a life and a power of its own. 2. Hegemony.  Antonio Gramsci , the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, argued that the ruling class rules not by coercion alone but by  hegemony  — intellectual and moral leadership manufactured through  civil society : school, church, press and popular culture. Through them the existing distribution of property comes to look like natural ‘common sense’, so that consent rather than the policeman keeps the order standing. 3. False consciousness and the war of position.  The result is  false consciousness : the exploited understand their own condition in categories supplied by their exploiters — the worker who votes for his employer’s party has borrowed his employer’s worldview. Revolution therefore requires first a  war of position , a long ideological struggle in which  organic intellectuals  thrown up by the working class build a counter-hegemony, before any frontal ‘war of manoeuvre’ can succeed. 4. The Frankfurt School.  Horkheimer ,  Adorno  and  Marcuse  made three contributions:    4.1 Critical theory  — Marxism recast as a critique of culture, reason and domination rather than of economics alone.    4.2 The ‘culture industry’  — art and leisure are turned into standardised commodities that pacify rather than provoke.    4.3 One-dimensional man  —  Marcuse’s   One-Dimensional Man  shows how advanced capitalism manufactures ‘false needs’ and absorbs dissent — selling the discontented a new phone instead of a new society — so that opposition itself becomes a commodity. 5. Althusser.  Louis Althusser , of the structuralist school, allowed each level relative autonomy in a ‘multi-sectoral’ analysis, the economy being determinant only ‘in the last instance’. Two devices carry his account of ideology:    5.1 Ideological state apparatuses  — family, school, religion and media, which reproduce the relations of production far more quietly than the repressive apparatus of army and police.    5.2 Interpellation  — the process by which ideology ‘hails’ individuals and constitutes them as obedient subjects. 6. Conclusion.  Neo-Marxism shifted the decisive battleground from the  economy to culture and consciousness . In doing so it explained capitalism’s remarkable durability and reshaped Marxism into a theory of ideology and hegemony rather than of inevitable economic collapse — the form in which Marxism still influences media studies, education and cultural politics today. Q — Why is the sex/gender distinction central to feminist analysis? Distinguish liberal, socialist and radical feminism and the waves of feminism. (UPSC 2012/2019) What it’s asking:  Two halves — why sex/gender is the foundation of feminist argument, and how the strands and the three waves differ. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  — feminism rests on two beliefs: ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’. 2. Sex vs gender  — sex is biological and fixed,  gender  a changeable social construct;  Beauvoir : ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’.  (Sex is who bears the child; gender is the rule that the daughter cooks while the son studies.) 3. Liberal feminism  —  Wollstonecraft, Mill, Friedan : equal legal and political rights within the system, since gender is ‘irrelevant to public life’.  (Equal education, the vote, equal pay for equal work.) 4. Socialist & radical  — two structural explanations of subordination:    4.1 Socialist feminism  —  Engels  ties patriarchy to  capitalism  (women as a ‘reserve army of labour’).  (The unpaid cooking and care that sends the wage-earner back to work each morning costs capital nothing.)    4.2 Radical feminism  —  Millett  locates it in  patriarchy  itself — ‘the personal is political’. 5. Three waves  — the movement in three phases:    5.1 First wave  — suffrage and legal rights.    5.2 Second wave (1961–91)  — women’s liberation and the private sphere.    5.3 Third wave (from the 1990s)  — difference: black, postcolonial and eco-feminism. 6. Conclusion  — the distinction converts subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice; the strands differ only on the cure. Model Answer 1. Core.  Feminist ideology rests on two beliefs — ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’. The first is descriptive and the second normative, which is why feminism is simultaneously a theory of society and a movement for its transformation, cutting across liberal, socialist and radical traditions rather than belonging to any one of them. 2. Sex versus gender.  The  sex/gender distinction  is central because  sex  denotes ineradicable biological difference, whereas  gender  is a cultural construct of masculine and feminine roles that society imposes and can therefore unmake. As  Simone de Beauvoir  put it, ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’: sex is who bears the child, gender is the household rule that the daughter cooks while the son studies. This shatters the claim that ‘biology is destiny’ and converts subordination into a social wrong. 3. Liberal feminism.  Mary Wollstonecraft  ( A Vindication of the Rights of Woman ),  J.S. Mill  and  Betty Friedan  are reformist: gender is ‘irrelevant to public life’, so women need equal education, the vote, equal legal personality and equal pay within the existing order. Critics answer that formal equality leaves the unequal burdens of the home untouched, and that it speaks chiefly for educated middle-class women. 4. Socialist and radical feminism.  Both go beyond legal equality to a structural explanation of women’s subordination, but locate its root differently:    4.1 Socialist feminism  —  Engels  ( The Origin of the Family ;  Juliet Mitchell ) ties patriarchy to  capitalism : women form a ‘reserve army of labour’ and their unpaid domestic work reproduces labour power free of cost to capital.    4.2 Radical feminism  —  Kate Millett, Germaine Greer, Beauvoir  reply that  patriarchy  is itself the root, prior to class — ‘the personal is political’ — so family, marriage and sexuality must be transformed, not merely property. 5. The three waves.  The movement is conventionally divided into three phases:    5.1 First wave (to the 1960s)  — the suffrage movement, winning legal personality and the vote.    5.2 Second wave (1961–91)  — ‘women’s liberation’, which carried the struggle into the private sphere:  Friedan’s  ‘problem with no name’ named the discontent of the suburban housewife.    5.3 Third wave (from the 1990s)  — the politics of difference, expressed through black, postcolonial and eco-feminism. 6. Conclusion.  The sex/gender distinction is the theoretical foundation of every feminist strand because it turns women’s subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice. What divides feminists is only the cure — equal rights, the end of capitalism, or the overthrow of patriarchy — not the diagnosis that gender is made, and therefore can be unmade. Q — “One is not born, but becomes, a woman.” Examine radical feminism and patriarchy, and evaluate eco-feminism and the newer strands (black, postcolonial). (UPSC 2017) What it’s asking:  Unpack Beauvoir’s line through radical feminism’s theory of patriarchy, then weigh the eco-, black and postcolonial challenges to it. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Patriarchy  —  Millett : a system in which ‘male shall dominate female, elder male shall dominate younger’, prior to class or race.  (Its unit is the family: property, surname and authority descend from father to son.) 2. The personal is political  — the private sphere is itself a structure of power.  (Who eats last, who does the unpaid housework, who decides a pregnancy — all are questions of politics, not of affection.) 3. Woman as the ‘Other’  —  Beauvoir ,  The Second Sex : woman is defined only against man, so she is made, not born;  Brownmiller : ‘rape is an institution of patriarchy’. 4. Eco-feminism  —  d’Eaubonne ,  Vandana Shiva ,  Mary Daly : woman and nature are both treated as passive resources.  (The Indian village woman who fetches the water and gathers the fuel is the first to suffer when the forest and the stream are destroyed.) 5. Black & postcolonial  — mainstream feminism universalised the white middle-class woman and ignored race and class; two challengers:    5.1 Black feminism  —  bell hooks : race and class cut across any common sisterhood.    5.2 Postcolonial feminism  —  Chandra Talpade Mohanty : the ‘third-world woman’ cannot be spoken for by Western feminists. 6. Conclusion  — feminism moves from sisterhood-as-sameness to a  politics of difference . Model Answer 1. Patriarchy.  Radical feminism, the defining strand of the  second wave , holds that  patriarchy  — literally ‘rule by the father’ — is the most fundamental and universal form of oppression, older and deeper than class or race.  Kate Millett  defines it as a system in which ‘male shall dominate female, elder male shall dominate younger’; its basic unit is the family, through which property, surname and authority descend from father to son. 2. The personal is political.  Its rallying idea,  ‘the personal is political’ , denies the liberal separation of public and private: the family, marriage, housework and sexuality are themselves structures of power. Who eats last, who performs the unpaid domestic labour and who decides a pregnancy are political questions, not matters of private affection — which is why domestic violence and marital rape became feminist causes rather than family secrets. 3. Woman as the ‘Other’.  Simone de Beauvoir  ( The Second Sex ) argues that man is posited as the norm and woman defined only in relation to him — the  ‘Other’  — so that ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’: femininity is manufactured by upbringing, not given by nature.  Susan Brownmiller  pressed the argument further, calling rape ‘an institution of patriarchy’, and some radicals advocate androgyny as the escape. 4. Eco-feminism.  Credited to  Francoise d’Eaubonne  and developed by  Vandana Shiva  and  Mary Daly , eco-feminism links the  domination of women  with the  domination of nature : a masculinist, exploitative order treats both as passive resources to be used up. For Shiva the Indian village woman who fetches the water and gathers the fuel is the first casualty when forest and stream are destroyed, which makes women the natural allies of ecology. 5. Black and postcolonial feminism.  Both charge that mainstream white, middle-class feminism universalised one experience and ignored  race and class :    5.1 Black feminism  —  bell hooks  argues that the woman who must also fight poverty, caste and racism does not share the suburban housewife’s agenda.    5.2 Postcolonial feminism  —  Chandra Talpade Mohanty  holds that the ‘third-world woman’, burdened by a colonial legacy, cannot be spoken for by Western feminists. 6. Conclusion.  Radical feminism transformed the discipline by politicising the private sphere, but its assumption of a single ‘women’s experience’ — an ‘essential’ femininity — is exactly what eco-, black and postcolonial feminists contest. Feminism has accordingly moved from sisterhood-as-sameness to a  politics of difference . Q — Is fascism a coherent ideology? Discuss its anti-rationalism and core tenets, its conception of the state, and whether it was merely an inter-war phenomenon. What it’s asking:  Test whether fascism is an ideology at all — its anti-rational core, its state, and whether it died in 1945. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core  — from  fasces , ‘strength through unity’: ‘the individual, in a literal sense, is nothing’; a ‘hodge-podge of ideologies’ rather than a system.  (No founding text answers to Marx’s Capital or Locke’s Treatises.) 2. Anti-rationalism  — a counter-Enlightenment cult of will, instinct and myth over reason:  Sorel’s  ‘political myths’, ‘action not talk’, ‘1789 is dead’.  (Torchlit parades, uniforms and the myth of national rebirth move the crowd where argument cannot.) 3. Struggle & leadership  — three further core tenets:    3.1 Struggle  — social Darwinism: ‘war is to men what maternity is to women’.    3.2 Leadership & elitism  — the Führerprinzip, drawing on  Nietzsche’s  Übermensch.    3.3 Ultranationalism  — chauvinistic, ranking nations as organic and unequal wholes. 4. The state  — totalitarian and  corporatist ;  Mussolini  and  Gentile : ‘nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it’.  (State-licensed bodies of employers and workers replace free trade unions — class conflict abolished by decree.) 5. Merely inter-war?  — three rival explanations:    5.1  Nolte  — ties it to defeat, depression and fear of communism, so it died with its epoch.    5.2  Fromm  — to the ‘fear of freedom’ in human nature, which implies recurrence.    5.3  Laski  — ‘capitalism defending itself’. 6. Conclusion  — not a coherent ideology but a reactive movement; its impulses recur wherever crisis breeds authoritarian nationalism. Model Answer 1. Core.  Fascism takes its name from the  fasces , the bundle of rods symbolising ‘strength through unity’, and subordinates the individual utterly to nation and state — ‘the individual, in a literal sense, is nothing’ — aiming to forge a ‘new man’ of duty and sacrifice. Having no founding text comparable to  Capital  or  Two Treatises of Government , it is commonly dismissed as a ‘ hodge-podge of ideologies ’ or a ‘political religion’ rather than a coherent doctrine. 2. Anti-rationalism.  Anti-rationalism  is its hallmark: a counter-Enlightenment cult of  will, instinct and myth  in place of reason.  Georges Sorel’s  ‘political myths’ supply the model — a belief is judged by its power to mobilise, not by its truth — and Mussolini preferred ‘action, not talk’, declaring that ‘1789 is dead’. Torchlit parades, uniforms and the myth of national rebirth were deliberately chosen to move crowds where argument could not. 3. Struggle and leadership.  Its other tenets follow, among them the pseudo-radical appeal of ‘national socialism’:    3.1 Struggle  — conflict as the law of life, a social Darwinism in which ‘war is to men what maternity is to women’.    3.2 Leadership and elitism  — the Führerprinzip, by which the leader embodies the will of the people, drawing on  Nietzsche’s  Übermensch.    3.3 Ultranationalism  — a chauvinistic creed that ranks nations as organic and unequal wholes. 4. The state.  Fascism’s state is  totalitarian  and  corporatist . For  Mussolini  and  Giovanni Gentile  there is ‘nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it’, an inheritance from Hegel’s worship of the state. Corporatism means that state-licensed bodies of employers and workers replace free trade unions, so class conflict is abolished by decree rather than resolved. Nazism added  racialism  — Aryan supremacy, anti-Semitism and the ‘final solution’. 5. Merely inter-war?  Three rival explanations are offered:    5.1  Ernst Nolte  — treats fascism as the product of specific  inter-war circumstances  — military defeat, the Depression, wounded national pride and fear of communism — so that it died with its epoch.    5.2  Erich Fromm  — locates it instead in human nature, in the ‘fear of freedom’ that tempts the insecure individual to surrender himself to an authority, which implies recurrence.    5.3  Laski  — offers the Marxist reading: ‘a desperate attempt by capitalism to protect itself’. 6. Conclusion.  Fascism is best seen not as a coherent ideology but as a reactive, anti-rational movement of extreme nationalism and leader-worship, held together by enemies rather than by principles. Fromm’s ‘fear of freedom’ is the warning: it was no mere inter-war accident, and its impulses resurface wherever crisis breeds authoritarian nationalism.
